column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 29: “The gates of good”

column2: From Muʿādh (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, tell me of a deed that will take me into Paradise and keep me far from the Fire. He said:

“You have asked about something great, yet it is easy for one for whom Allah makes it easy: worship Allah without associating anything with Him, keep up the prayer, give zakāh, fast Ramaḍān and make the Ḥajj to the House.”
Then he said: “Shall I not direct you to the gates of good?

Fasting is a shield; charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and a man's prayer in the depth of the night.” Then he recited: “Their sides forsake their beds…” until he reached “…what they used to do” [al-Sajdah 32:16–17]. Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and the peak of its hump?”

I said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and the peak of its hump is jihād.” Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?”
I said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He took hold of his tongue and said: “Restrain this.” I said: Prophet of Allah, will we really be taken to account for what we say?
He said: “May your mother be bereft of you! Is there anything that topples people into the Fire on their faces” — or he said, “on their noses” — “but the harvests of their tongues?”
Al-Tirmidhī reported it, and said: A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.

This hadith was recorded by Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah through the narration of Maʿmar, from ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, from Abū Wāʾil, from Muʿādh ibn Jabal. Al-Tirmidhī said: Ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
What he (may Allah have mercy on him) said is open to question on two counts.

First, it has not been established that Abū Wāʾil heard from Muʿādh, even though he was old enough to have met him. Muʿādh was in al-Shām and Abū Wāʾil in al-Kūfah, and the imams, such as Aḥmad and others, have always taken things like this as evidence that there was no hearing.
Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said of Abū Wāʾil's hearing from Abū al-Dardāʾ: He lived in his time, but he was in al-Kūfah and Abū al-Dardāʾ in al-Shām — meaning that his hearing from him is not authenticated.
Abū Zurʿah al-Dimashqī related that some people suspended judgement on Abū Wāʾil's hearing from ʿUmar, or denied it; so his hearing from Muʿādh is even less likely.
Second, Ḥammād ibn Salamah reported it from ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Muʿādh; Imam Aḥmad recorded it in brief. Al-Dāraquṭnī said: That is closer to being correct,
because the hadith is known through the narration of Shahr, though it has been reported from him in differing ways.

I say: Shahr's narration from Muʿādh is certainly mursal, and Shahr is disputed, some declaring him trustworthy and others weak. Imam Aḥmad recorded it through the narration of Shahr, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm, from Muʿādh.

Imam Aḥmad also recorded it through the narration of ʿUrwah ibn al-Nazzāl — or al-Nazzāl ibn ʿUrwah — and Maymūn ibn Abī Shabīb, both from Muʿādh; but neither ʿUrwah nor Maymūn heard from Muʿādh. It has other routes from Muʿādh, all of them weak.

His words, “Tell me of a deed that will take me into Paradise and keep me far from the Fire”: we saw above, in the commentary on the twenty-second hadith, from established routes in the hadiths of Abū Hurayrah, Abū Ayyūb and others,
that the Prophet ﷺ was asked a question like this and answered much as he answered in the hadith of Muʿādh.

In Imam Aḥmad's narration of the hadith of Muʿādh, he said: Messenger of Allah, I want to ask you about something that has made me ill, sick and sorrowful. He said: “Ask about whatever you wish.” He said: Tell me of a deed that will take me into Paradise; I will ask you about nothing else.

This shows how deeply concerned Muʿādh (may Allah be pleased with him) was with righteous deeds. It is also evidence that deeds are a cause of entering Paradise, as the Exalted says: “That is the Paradise you have been given to inherit for what you used to do” [al-Zukhruf 43:72].

As for his saying ﷺ, “None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds,” what is meant — and Allah knows best — is that no one would deserve Paradise by the deed itself, were it not that Allah, by His bounty and mercy, has made it a cause of that;
and the deed itself is part of Allah's mercy and bounty to His servant. So Paradise and its causes are all from Allah's bounty and mercy.

His words, “You have asked about something great”: we saw above, in the commentary on that hadith, that the Prophet ﷺ said to a man who asked him something like this: “Though you have put the question briefly,

you have asked about something great and far-reaching.” That is because entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire is a very great matter; it was for this that Allah sent down the Books and sent the messengers. The Prophet ﷺ said to a man: “What do you say when you pray?”

He said: I ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire; I cannot do your murmuring (dandanah) or Muʿādh's murmuring — referring to how much they supplicated and how hard they strove in their requests. The Prophet ﷺ said: “It is around these that we murmur.”
In one narration: “Does my murmuring and Muʿādh's murmuring come to anything but our asking Allah for Paradise and seeking refuge with Him from the Fire?”

His words, “yet it is easy for one for whom Allah makes it easy,” indicate that success lies entirely in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever Allah makes guidance easy for is guided, and whoever He does not make it easy for will not find it so. Allah the Exalted says:

“As for one who gives, fears [Allah] and affirms the best, We shall ease him towards ease; but as for one who is miserly, thinks himself self-sufficient and denies the best, We shall ease him towards hardship” [al-Layl 92:5–10]. And he ﷺ said: “Act, for everyone is eased towards what he was created for:
the people of happiness are eased towards the deeds of the people of happiness, and the people of misery are eased towards the deeds of the people of misery.” Then he ﷺ recited this verse.
In his supplication the Prophet ﷺ used to say: “Guide me and make guidance easy for me.” And Allah has told of His prophet Mūsā (peace be upon him) that he said in his supplication:
“My Lord, open my breast for me and make my task easy for me” [Ṭā Hā 20:25–26]. Ibn ʿUmar used to supplicate: O Allah, ease me towards ease and keep me away from hardship.
In the commentary on that hadith we have already explained why entering Paradise is made to depend on performing the five pillars of Islam, which are tawḥīd, prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj.

His words, “Shall I not direct you to the gates of good?”: having made entering Paradise depend on the obligations of Islam, he then directed him to the gates of good among the voluntary deeds. For the best of Allah's friends (awliyāʾ) are those brought near, who seek nearness to Him through voluntary deeds after fulfilling the obligatory ones.
His words, “Fasting is a shield”: this saying is established from the Prophet ﷺ by many routes. It is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah,
from the Prophet ﷺ, and Imam Aḥmad recorded it with an addition: “Fasting is a shield and a strong fortress against the Fire.”
He also recorded, from the hadith of ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Fasting is a shield against the Fire, like the shield any of you has in battle.”
And from the hadith of Jābir, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Our Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, said: Fasting is a shield with which the servant shields himself from the Fire.”

Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Abū ʿUbaydah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Fasting is a shield so long as one does not tear it.” By “so long as one does not tear it” he means: tear it with evil speech and the like.

That is why, in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Fasting is a shield. So when it is a day of fasting for one of you, let him not speak obscenely or behave ignorantly; and if someone insults him, let him say: I am fasting.”
One of the Salaf said: Backbiting tears the fast, and seeking forgiveness patches it; so whoever of you can avoid coming with a torn fast, let him do so.
Ibn al-Munkadir said: When the fasting person backbites, he tears [his fast]; and when he seeks forgiveness, he patches it.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain open to question, from Abū Hurayrah as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ): “Fasting is a shield so long as one does not tear it.” He was asked: With what does one tear it?
He said: “With lying or backbiting.”

The shield (junnah) is that with which the servant shields himself, like the shield (mijann) that protects him from blows in battle. In the same way fasting protects the one who fasts from sins in this world,
as the Mighty and Majestic says: “O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful of Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:183].
If he has a shield against sins, he will have a shield against the Fire in the Hereafter; and if he has no shield against sins in this world, he will have no shield against the Fire in the Hereafter.
Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from the hadith of ʿAlī as marfūʿ: “Allah sent Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā to the Children of Israel with five words,” and he related the hadith in full. In it:
“Allah commands you to fast. The likeness of that is a man who walks towards his enemy having taken a shield for the fight, so that he has no fear from whatever direction he is attacked.”

He recorded it by another route from ʿAlī as mawqūf (his own words), and in it he said: “Fasting is like a man on whom people set out to take revenge, and who armed himself so thoroughly that he thought the enemy's weapons would never reach him; in the same way fasting is a shield.”
His words, “and charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire”: this saying has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by other routes.
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded it from the hadith of Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Fasting is a strong shield, and charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire.”
Al-Ṭabarānī and others recorded it from the hadith of Anas as marfūʿ, with the same meaning.
Al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, recorded from the hadith of Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Secret charity extinguishes the Lord's anger and wards off an evil death.”

It is narrated of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn that he used to carry bread on his back at night, seeking out the poor with it in the darkness of the night, and would say: Charity in the darkness of the night extinguishes the anger of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “If you disclose your charities, that is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you, and He will remove some of your bad deeds from you” [al-Baqarah 2:271]. This shows that bad deeds are expiated by charity: either by charity in general, or by secret charity.
His words, “and a man's prayer in the depth of the night”, mean that it too extinguishes sin, like charity. This is shown by what Imam Aḥmad recorded through the narration of ʿUrwah ibn al-Nazzāl,

from Muʿādh, who said: We were returning with the Prophet ﷺ from the expedition of Tabūk — and he related the hadith, in which: “Fasting is a shield, and charity and the servant's standing [in prayer] in the depth of the night expiate sin.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best prayer after the prescribed prayer is the night prayer.”

It has been narrated from a number of the Companions that people are set burning by their sins during the day, and each time they stand for one of the prescribed prayers they extinguish their sins. This has been narrated as marfūʿ by routes open to question.
In the same way the night prayer expiates sins,
because it is the best of voluntary prayers. In al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Bilāl, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Keep to the night prayer,

for it was the practice of the righteous before you; and the night prayer is a means of nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, a restraint from sin, an expiation for bad deeds and a driver of disease from the body.”
He also recorded it from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, from the Prophet ﷺ, in similar terms, and said: It is more authentic than the hadith of Bilāl.
Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Ḥākim recorded it in their Ṣaḥīḥs, also from the hadith of Abū Umāmah.
Ibn Masʿūd said: The superiority of prayer at night over prayer by day is like the superiority of secret charity over open charity.
Abū Nuʿaym recorded it from him as marfūʿ, but the mawqūf version (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ) is more authentic.
It has already been mentioned that secret charity extinguishes sin and extinguishes the Lord's anger; and so does the night prayer.

His words, “Then he recited: ‘Their sides forsake their beds as they call on their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend from what We have provided them. No soul knows what joy has been kept hidden for them, as a reward for what they used to do’ [al-Sajdah 32:16–17],” mean

that the Prophet ﷺ recited these two verses when mentioning the merit of the night prayer, in order to make its merit clear. It has been narrated from Anas that this verse was revealed about waiting for the ʿishāʾ prayer; al-Tirmidhī recorded it and declared it authentic.
It is narrated from him that he said of this verse: They used to pray voluntary prayers between maghrib and ʿishāʾ. Abū Dāwūd recorded it.
Something similar is narrated from Bilāl; al-Bazzār recorded it with a weak chain.

All of this falls within the general wording of the verse, for Allah praised those whose sides forsake their beds to call on Him. That includes everyone who gives up sleep at night to remember Allah and call on Him, so it includes whoever prays between the two evening prayers [maghrib and ʿishāʾ],

and whoever waits for the ʿishāʾ prayer and does not sleep until he has prayed it, especially when he needs sleep and struggles against himself to forgo it in order to perform the obligatory prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said to those who were waiting for the ʿishāʾ prayer: “You remain in prayer so long as you are waiting for the prayer.”
It also includes one who sleeps and then rises from his sleep at night for the night vigil (tahajjud), which is the best kind of voluntary prayer without qualification.

Perhaps it also includes one who gives up sleep at the break of dawn and rises to perform the dawn prayer, especially when sleep is overpowering him. That is why the muezzin is prescribed to say in the dawn call to prayer: Prayer is better than sleep.

His words ﷺ, “and a man's prayer in the depth of the night”, name the best time for the night vigil: the depth of the night. Al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, who said: Someone asked: Messenger of Allah, which supplication is most heard?
He said: “In the depth of the last part of the night, and at the end of the prescribed prayers.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it from the hadith of Abū Dharr, who said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ which part of the night is best.
He said: “The best of the night is its depth.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Muslim, who said: I said to Abū Dharr: Which night prayer is best?
He said: I asked the Prophet ﷺ as you have asked me, and he said:
“The depth of the remaining night” — or “the middle of the night” — “and few are those who do it.”
Al-Bazzār and al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was asked: In which part of the night is supplication most readily answered?
He said: “In the depth of the night.” In his narration al-Bazzār added: “the last part.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “The Lord is nearest to the servant in the depth of the last part of the night;

so if you can be among those who remember Allah at that hour, then be so.” He declared it authentic. Imam Aḥmad recorded it with the wording: He said: I said: Messenger of Allah, which hours are best?

He said: “The depth of the last part of the night.” In another narration of his: “The depth of the last part of the night is when supplication is most readily answered.” And in another narration of his: I said: Messenger of Allah, is there any hour nearer to Allah than another?
He said: “The depth of the last part of the night.”

Ibn Mājah recorded it, and in his version: “the depth of the middle of the night.” In a narration of Imam Aḥmad's from ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah, he said: I said: Messenger of Allah, is there any hour better than another?
He said: “Allah draws near in the depth of the night and forgives everything except shirk.”

It has been said that when “the depth of the night” is used without qualification, its middle is meant; and when “the depth of the last part of the night” is said, what is meant is the middle of the second half, which is the fifth sixth of the night. That is the time for which the divine descent is reported.
His words ﷺ: “Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and the peak of its hump?”

I said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He said: “The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and the peak of its hump is jihād.” In a narration of Imam Aḥmad's, through Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibn Ghanm, from Muʿādh, he said:

The Prophet of Allah ﷺ said to me: “If you wish, I will tell you of the head of this matter, what keeps this matter upright, and the peak of the hump.” I said: Certainly. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“The head of this matter is that you bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger; what keeps this matter upright is keeping up the prayer and giving zakāh; and the peak of its hump is jihād in the path of Allah.

I have been commanded only to fight people until they keep up the prayer, give zakāh and bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger. When they do that, they have sought protection and secured their blood and their wealth, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad, no face has grown pale and no foot has become dusty in any deed by which the degrees of Paradise are sought, after the obligatory prayer, like jihād in the path of Allah;
and nothing makes a servant's scale heavy like an animal of his that dies in the path of Allah, or on which [a fighter] is mounted in the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
So the Prophet ﷺ told of three things: the head of the matter, its pillar and the peak of its hump.

As for the head of the matter — by “the matter” he means the religion with which he was sent, namely Islam — it is explained in the other narration as the two testimonies. Whoever does not affirm them outwardly and inwardly has no part in Islam at all.

As for what keeps the religion upright, on which the religion stands as a tent stands on its pole, that is the prayer; in the other narration: “keeping up the prayer and giving zakāh.” We have already discussed the pillars of Islam and how they are bound to one another.
As for the peak of its hump — its highest and loftiest part — that is jihād. This shows that it is the best of deeds after the obligatory ones, as is the view of Imam Aḥmad and other scholars.

His words in Imam Aḥmad's narration, “By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad, no face has grown pale and no foot has become dusty in any deed by which the degrees of Paradise are sought, after the obligatory prayer, like jihād in the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic,” show this explicitly.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Dharr, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, which deed is best?
He said: “Faith in Allah and jihād in His path.”
Both also have, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The best of deeds is faith in Allah, then jihād in the path of Allah.”
The hadiths with this meaning are very many.
His words, “Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?” — I said: Certainly, Messenger of Allah. He took hold of his tongue and said: “Restrain this” — to the end of the hadith.

This shows that restraining the tongue, controlling it and holding it back is the root of all good, and that whoever controls his tongue has control of his affairs, and has made them firm and kept them in order.
This meaning has already been discussed in the commentary on the hadith, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent,”
and in the commentary on the hadith, “Say: I believe in Allah, then remain steadfast.”
Al-Bazzār recorded in his Musnad, from the hadith of Abū al-Yasar, that a man said: Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed that will take me into Paradise. He said:

“Hold this back,” and he pointed to his tongue. The man repeated the question, and he said: “May your mother be bereft of you! Does anything topple people on their noses into the Fire but the harvests of their tongues?” Al-Bazzār said: Its chain is ḥasan.
What is meant by the harvests of the tongues is the recompense and the punishments for forbidden speech;

for by his words and deeds a person sows good deeds and bad deeds, and then on the Day of Resurrection he reaps what he sowed. Whoever sows good in word or deed reaps honour, and whoever sows evil in word or deed will reap regret tomorrow.

The apparent sense of the hadith of Muʿādh indicates that what most often takes people into the Fire is speaking with their tongues. For the sins of speech include shirk, the greatest of sins in the sight of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; they include speaking about Allah without knowledge, which is the companion of shirk;

they include false testimony, which has been made equal to associating partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and they include sorcery, slanderous accusation (qadhf) and other major and minor sins, such as lying, backbiting and talebearing. And the other sins, those of action, are seldom free of some speech that accompanies them and helps them along.
In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “What most often takes people into the Fire is the two hollow things: the mouth and the private parts.” Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded it.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man may speak a word without considering what is in it, and by it slip into the Fire farther than the distance between the east and the west.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded it with the wording: “A man may speak a word in which he sees no harm, and by it fall seventy autumns into the Fire.”

Mālik reported, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that ʿUmar came in on Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with them both) while he was pulling at his tongue. ʿUmar said: Stop! May Allah forgive you!
Abū Bakr said: This has brought me to the places of ruin.

Ibn Buraydah said: I saw Ibn ʿAbbās holding his tongue and saying: Woe to you! Speak good and you will gain, or keep silent about evil and you will be safe; otherwise, know that you will regret it. The narrator said: Someone said to him: Ibn ʿAbbās, why do you say this?

He said: It has reached me that a person — I think he said — will not be more furious or enraged with any part of his body on the Day of Resurrection than with his tongue, except one who spoke good with it or dictated good with it.
Ibn Masʿūd used to swear by Allah, besides whom there is no god: There is nothing on earth more in need of long imprisonment than a tongue.
Al-Ḥasan said: The tongue is the commander of the body. When it commits an offence, the limbs commit offences; and when it is chaste, they are chaste.
Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd said: I have never seen anyone keep watch over his tongue without seeing the effect of it as soundness in the rest of his deeds.
Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: Whenever a man's speech was sound, I could see it in the rest of his deeds; and whenever a man's speech was corrupt, I could always see that in the rest of his deeds.

Al-Mubārak ibn Faḍālah reported that Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd said: There is no single act of righteousness that brings all other righteousness in its train except [guarding] the tongue. You find a man who fasts by day

and breaks his fast on what is unlawful, who prays at night and bears false witness by day — and he mentioned other things like this — but you will never find one who speaks only the truth and whose deeds then go against that.
